newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian market hails Svyazinvest sale.
newsitem.headline: Russian market hails Svyazinvest sale.

text.p: Russian telecoms shares surged 10 percent and more on Monday in a thumping vote of approval for the government's sale of a quarter of telecoms holding company Svyazinvest for a higher than expected $1.875 billion.

Analysts hailed Friday's sale -- Russia's biggest ever privatisation -- as generally fair and open, but the tender results sparked a vicious war of words between Russian bankers and tycoons, fought out in the media they control.
"It's definitely the best privatisation deal I've seen," said Anton Inshutin, telecoms analyst at CentreInvest Securities.
First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov dismissed the complaints of the losers, saying the winner had offered enough for Russia to pay off its wage arrears to the public sector.
"Those that lost, instead of taking it calmly, have gone into hysterics on television," he said.

And for all the transparency of the tender process and the good price, analysts regretted that the winning consortium did not include a foreign telecoms operator, whose experience could lead the ramshackle Russian telephone industry into the future.

The 25 percent plus one share stake in Svyazinvest was won by a consortium built around Uneximbank, Russia's third biggest bank, and Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (DMG), the London-based investment banking division of Germany's Deutsche Bank.
"A good price... but the wrong people won. There wasn't a telephone company among them," said Philip Manduca, chief investment officer, emerging markets, at Eldon Capital Management in London.

The other $1.71 billion bid was from a consortium including Spain's Telefonica. Sources at Russia's Alfa-Bank and Most-Bank said their banks were bidding, and Russian news agencies said international investment bank CS First Boston was part of the losing consortium.
"The bad thing is that Telefonica lost the tender. I think Telefonica... as a telecoms operator would have been a much more valuable partner for Svyazinvest," said Inshutin.

The winning Mustcom consortium secured the shares in Svyazinvest, which owns controlling stakes in 88 phone companies including long-distance operator Rostelekom RTKM.RTS, with a bid well over the consensus forecast of about $1.5 billion and well in excess of the $1.18 billion starting price.

Uneximbank has said it wants to hold on to Svyazinvest as a strategic investment, but some analysts feel that DMG and Renaissance Capital, a Moscow investment bank also in the consortium, will want to increase and then realise its value.

"They'll want to see how the share price (of the local telecoms) reacts. When the share price rises they could offer (Svyazinvest) to large institutional investors at even higher prices," said Inshutin.
They did not have long to wait.
Rostelekom rose to $5.40 from $4.90 on Friday, and MGTS, the Moscow provider, rose to $2.30 from $2.03, with about $20 million changing hands in both stocks.

The higher than expected price for Svyazinvest led to a re-rating of the entire telecoms sector, which has in any case been one of the main targets of foreign investors in recent weeks, especially its second-tier regional stocks.

Inshutin estimates, on the basis of the price paid for Svyazinvest, that its price/sales ratio for 1996, consolidated on the basis of 38 percent stakes in its subsidiaries, is 3.3, against an industry average of 2.8.
Svyazinvest's market capitalisation per line, adjusted to exclude Rostelekom, which does not have its own lines, is $690, against an industry average of $590.

The winners are under no obligation to invest further in Svyazinvest, and Viktor Malin, deputy chairman of the Russian Federal Property Fund, which sold the stake, specifically said on Friday that they could do what they like with it, including selling it, once they have paid in full.
That would be from October 13 if payments are made on schedule.
Uneximbank may prefer to hold on to the shares, however.
A test of its intentions will come later this year or next, if it bids when the government sells another 24 percent stake in Svyazinvest, reducing state share to 51 percent.
The bank is already active in Russian privatisation, helped by the good government connections of its president, 36-year-old Vladimir Potanin, a former first deputy prime minister.
It is currently auctioning a 38 percent stake in metals group Norilsk Nickel, which it holds in trust for the government, and has said it intends to bid for ownership.
"Generally these companies are buying stakes and are restructuring rather than (asset) stripping. I expect they'll try to acquire the next stake when it comes on offer," said Manduca.
